newsitem.title: USA: HP outlines roadmap, sees performance boost.
newsitem.headline: HP outlines roadmap, sees performance boost.

text.p: Senior executives of Hewlett-Packard Co on Monday outlined the roadmap for HP's future computing systems, saying customers can expect up to 15 times greater performance over the next five years.

The executives, briefing reporters at company headquarters, said Hewlett-Packard plans to ease customers into new technologies that will support both its own blend of the Unix operating system and Microsoft's Windows NT.
The company said it plans to introduce fast new systems with greater multiprocessing capabilities as early as May.

Dick Watts, a vice president and general manager of HP's computer systems division, said the company and Intel Corp plan in coming months to unveil greater details about the new families of processors they are jointly developing.

HP and Intel are jointly developing a new generation of processors which are due to kick off with the Merced chip, initially expected as early as mid-1998, but which analysts now say should be on the market by the latter half of 1999.

The processors are based on 64-bit technology -- a faster architecture than Intel's current 32-bit chips -- although HP said its future systems would support programs that run on existing Intel 32-bit X86 chips and its own PA-RISC systems. HP Vice President Richard Sevcik said the nation's second largest computer company was seeking to preserve customers' investments in computer systems by ensuring that future technology works with existing software, but at increased performance.

Future systems will combine access to some 15,000 programs for the HP-UX version of Unix, with around 35,000 programs that run on current Intel-based machines. Over the next five years, HP systems will produce "between five times and 15 times more performance," with machines that can be used to design whole aircraft or cars, rather than just parts.

Outlining what HP is calling it's new "pervasive solutions foundation", he said HP expects this combined Unix-NT strategy to help it outdo rivals in the fiercely contested Unix market -- like Sun Microsystems Inc, Digital Equipment Corp and International Business Machines Corp..
"The cost of ownership's going to go down simply because there's a more homogeneous environment," Sevcik said. "We truly believe that this is going to become pervasive."

HP is expected to introduce a six-way symmetrical multiprocessing (SMP) machine in coming weeks, followed by an eight-way SMP midrange machine and, eventually, build up to a 32-way SMP high-end machine, rising to a 256-way SMP system.

The 256-processor SMP configuration, which would utilize a computing capability known as "crossbar technology" to crunch masses of data simultaneously, would be the type of system for advanced graphics designs, the executives said.
The road map also envisions parallel processing with machines packed with up to 4096 processors for use in warehousing masses of data.
HP will continue to produce its own PA-8000 series computer chips even after it begins shipping the new Intel chips in its fastest computers sometime in 1999.
A faster 8200 processor is due this year and an 8500 line due by mid-1998, HP executives said. The company is also moving to a 64-bit version of Unix later this year.
The HP executives said they would also work with Microsoft to develop what it called "a common cockpit" to help software developers write for both Unix and NT platforms.

Andrew Allison, an industry consultant and editor of Inside the New Computer Industry, said after the briefing that even if HP's performance improvements track with the rest of the industry, its Intel-based processor strategy could give it advantages in both costs and volume production capabilities.

"The reality is that performance has been doubling every 18 months," he said, referring to overall microprocessor performance in the industry. "I think this is a very logical story that they're talking about."
